steps.body: An equation like x = 5 has exactly ONE solution. An **inequality** like x > 5 has **infinitely many** — every number bigger than 5 works: 6, 7, 100, 5.001, all of them. Instead of pinning down one value, an inequality describes a whole range.

widget.prompt: Is x = 6 a solution of x > 5?

choices.label: Yes — 6 is greater than 5
choices.feedback: Right — 6 > 5 is true, so 6 solves the inequality.

choices.label: No — 6 doesn't equal 5
choices.feedback: The inequality doesn't ask for EQUALITY — it asks for GREATER THAN. 6 > 5 is true, so 6 works.

choices.label: Can't tell
choices.feedback: You can always tell — just check: is 6 greater than 5? Yes, so it's a solution.

steps.body: Because infinitely many numbers work, you can never list them all — but you can describe them completely with the inequality itself, or picture them on a number line (next lesson). The four symbols: **>** (greater than), **<** (less than), **≥** (greater than or equal), **≤** (less than or equal). The ≥ and ≤ symbols DO include the boundary value.

explanationVariants: ≤ means "less than OR equal to," so 3 qualifies since 3 = 3.
The equal-to part of ≤ includes the boundary itself.

widget.prompt: Is x = 3 a solution of x ≤ 3?

choices.label: Yes — ≤ includes the boundary value
choices.feedback: Right — ≤ means "less than OR equal to," and 3 equals 3, so it qualifies.

choices.label: No — 3 is not less than 3
choices.feedback: 3 isn't strictly LESS than 3, but ≤ also allows EQUAL — and 3 = 3, so it's included.

choices.label: Need more information
choices.feedback: ≤ is defined precisely: less than OR equal to. Since 3 = 3, it satisfies the "or equal" part.

explanationVariants: For x > 5, there's no biggest solution — for any number you pick, an even bigger one also works.

widget.prompt: What is the LARGEST solution of x > 5?

choices.label: There isn't one — solutions go on forever
choices.feedback: Right — for any number you name, say 1000, an even bigger one (1001) also solves x > 5. There's no largest.

explanationVariants: "At least 12" translates to t ≥ 12, which INCLUDES 12 itself — so 12 tickets qualifies.
"At least" is inclusive language, matching the ≥ symbol.

widget.prompt: A club needs "at least 12" members to run a trip: t ≥ 12. Does exactly t = 12 satisfy this?

choices.label: Yes — "at least" includes the exact number
choices.feedback: Right — "at least 12" means 12 or more, so t = 12 exactly satisfies t ≥ 12.

choices.label: No — you need MORE than 12
choices.feedback: "At least" is inclusive, matching ≥, not the strict >. Exactly 12 does qualify.

choices.label: Only if it's a round number
choices.feedback: It has nothing to do with roundness — ≥ simply includes the boundary. t = 12 satisfies t ≥ 12.

steps.body: A whole range, not one number.
takeaways: An inequality has infinitely many solutions — a range, not a single value.
Strict symbols (>, <) exclude the boundary; ≥ and ≤ include it.
"At least" and "at most" are inclusive language, matching ≥ and ≤.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Strict symbols exclude the boundary; ≥/≤ include it.** For x > 3, the number 3 itself does NOT qualify (3 is not greater than 3). For x ≥ 3, it DOES qualify (3 equals 3).

The boundary itself never satisfies a strict >.
